records.name_note: Sources split on the primary common name: NC State Extension's dedicated species page ("Grape Hyacinth") and Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder ("grape hyacinth") both lead with the plain name, while RHS's rendered page subtitle for the same binomial instead reads "Armenian grape hyacinth." NC State's structured "is often confused with" module for this species lists Hyacinthus orientalis alongside Crocus, Hyacinthoides hispanica, and Scilla mischtschenkoana as look-alikes -- underscoring that Muscari armeniacum, despite sharing the word "hyacinth" in its common name, is a different genus from Hyacinthus orientalis. No admissible source's species-specific page was found that directly contrasts Muscari armeniacum with its trade-name siblings M. botryoides or M. neglectum; see unknowns.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's dedicated species page carries no structured Poison section (no Poison Symptoms, Toxic Principle, or Poison Part fields appear on this page); instead it tags the plant "#non-toxic for cats", "#non-toxic for horses", and "#non-toxic for dogs". RHS, by contrast, carries a single 'Potentially harmful' field with a general, animal-unscoped caution: "Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling", followed on a second line within that same field, prefixed "Pets:", by "Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers" -- a caution that names no specific animal (not cats or dogs by name). Sources therefore disagree on framing: NC State affirmatively tags the species non-toxic to cats and dogs specifically, while RHS issues only a general "not to be eaten" edibility/handling caution without naming cats or dogs.
unknowns: is_houseplant lands false, not null: no admissible source designates Muscari armeniacum a houseplant or carries a #houseplant tag, NC State's Plant Type field renders only Bulb and Herbaceous Perennial, and all three dedicated pages describe a hardy outdoor spring bulb (NC State lists USDA zones 4a-8b). The researcher left this null; null is not a value the schema accepts for a hardy garden bulb.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Poison Information for Zantedeschia aethiopica (under its Poisonous-to-Humans heading, human-scoped) rates Poison Severity as Medium, gives Poison Toxic Principle as calcium oxalate, gives Poison Symptoms as "Oral irritation, pain, and swelling of mouth, tongue, and lips, excessive drooling, stomach pain, vomiting (not horses), diarrhea, difficulty swallowing," lists Poison Part as Flowers, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Stems, and states Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Separately, under its own Problems field (not the Poisonous-to-Humans block), the same page tags the species Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, and Problem for Horses. RHS's Botanical Details add that the plant is "Harmful if eaten; skin/eye irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling," with a further note scoped only to a generic "Pets" category rather than naming cats or dogs specifically: "Pets: Harmful if eaten; skin/eye irritant - for further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants."
records.cool_rest_note: Missouri Botanical Garden's Culture notes advise lifting the rhizomes for winter: "Lift rhizomes in fall and store in a damp medium such as peat or immediately replant in containers to overwinter as a houseplant."

light_fc_min/light_fc_good and direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's Light field values ('Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', 'Dappled Sunlight') are the site-wide light-category legend text (confirmed identical wording on other NC State species pages), not species-specific prose, so no hour figure was extracted per the scope rule.

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0) all as acceptable Soil pH values (both extremes open-ended), and RHS's own Growing Conditions pH field states 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral,' so no ceiling can be read off the Neutral band's closed top per the pH rule.

soil_base left null: the admissible sources do not converge on one growing medium. NC State's Landscape Location field renders Container, Houseplants, Pond and Riparian; Missouri Botanical Garden's Uses field reads "Borders, containers, pond peripheries, water gardens or houseplants."; and RHS's Cultivation field -- which is this species page's own How-to-Grow text and species-specific throughout (it names this plant's 30cm marginal-aquatic depth, an aquatic compost and a planting basket), not the genus boilerplate that sits in RHS's separately labelled Genus field -- names three media at once: open ground ("moisture-retentive soil"), "peat-free John Innes No2 potting compost" in containers, and aquatic compost in a basket. NC State's Soil Texture list (Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt)) describes soil types, not a bed-versus-container decision. With this record's is_houseplant true, no single enum token is honest here, so the field is left null and the split disclosed. The earlier garden_bed value rested on a citation that invoked the Landscape Location field while quoting only Soil Texture, and that field contradicts it.

water_regime keep_moist rests on Missouri Botanical Garden's Culture prose ('Best in moist soils with full sun to part shade.', and plantable in up to 12" of water at a pond edge) and on NC State's own species prose, 'Plant in the full sun to partial shade in moist,  organically rich soil with plenty of leaf mold, rotted manure, and humus.', together with NC State's Soil Drainage field (Frequent Standing Water, Moist, Occasional Flooding, Occasionally Wet). Missouri Botanical Garden's structured Water field reads 'Medium to wet': only the lower end of that range sits below keep_moist and its upper end is direct support, so it is not a counterpoint. An earlier draft of this entry attributed the phrase 'Moist soil preferred' to NC State; that string is not on the page and has been removed.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, and all fertilize_* fields: no admissible source frames watering or feeding for this in-ground/bog perennial by a day interval, soil-check depth, dilution strength, or active-month schedule.

The name 'African Lily' (one of NC State's alphabetized Other Common Name(s) for this species) is also used elsewhere for the unrelated genus Agapanthus; this record does not assign it any priority and uses it only as one of several NC State-listed alternates for Zantedeschia aethiopica.

Colored florist callas (Z. elliottiana, Z. rehmannii and hybrids) and the genus-level Zantedeschia pages were deliberately excluded as sources; only content specific to the Zantedeschia aethiopica species page was used.

records.cool_rest_note: Missouri Botanical Garden notes that tubers may be left in the ground year-round in USDA Zones 8-10; in colder gardens (its example is St. Louis) they are planted in mid-spring, dug after the first fall frost and overwintered in a cool dry location where temperatures do not dip below 45°F, in somewhat the same manner as done for cannas.
records.name_note: NC State publishes this single species record under six common-name URLs -- Caladium, Dasheen, Elephant Ears, Green Taro, Malanga and Taro -- each rendering a different H1; the canonical page's H1 is the binomial and its alphabetized Other Common Name(s) list therefore opens with "Caladium". The Taro view is used here as the anchor, because "Caladium" and "Elephant Ears" both also belong to the unrelated species Caladium bicolor, whose own NC State page carries them in its Common Name(s) list, and because RHS independently leads with "taro" -- its Other common names list runs aivi, Arabian cocoa root, bleeding heart, callaloo, cocoyam, dalo, dasheen, eddo, Egyptian cocoa root, Egyptian ginger, elephant ears, imo, kalo, keladi, talas, and does not repeat taro. NC State's own Description for this species opens "Taro, or elephant ear, is a tender herbaceous perennial in the Araceae (arum) family with a clumping growth habit."
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Problems field for this species renders five values -- Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses -- and the Problem-for-Cats and Problem-for-Dogs tags are separate from the human-scoped Poison block below them. That block gives Poison Severity "Medium", Poison Toxic Principle "Calcium oxalate crystals", a complete six-part Poison Part list -- Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems -- and Poison Symptoms "Oral irritation, pain and swelling of mouth, tongue, and lips, excessive drooling, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing can result from eating parts of this plant. Causes an extremely unpleasant sensation similar to needles being stuck into the mouth and tongue. All parts of the plant are poisonous unless cooked first." NC State also carries "Poisonous" as one of the four values of its Plant Type field (Houseplant, Perennial, Poisonous, Water Plant). This species is a food crop as well as an ornamental, and the condition is the source's own: NC State's Edibility field states "Poisonous until cooked. Poisons neutralized by thoroughly drying or cooking the plant or by steeping it in water. Taro root used in Southeastern Asian cuisine.  Use salted water and boil for at least one hour." RHS adds a handling warning scoped to Humans/Pets without naming an animal: "Humans/Pets: Harmful if eaten; skin/eye irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling". The sources disagree on the contact hazard, and the disagreement is live: NC State's Poison block answers "Causes Contact Dermatitis: No", while RHS calls the plant a skin/eye irritant and a UGA CAES Field Report gives this species' toxicity class as "Oxalates, Dermatitis".

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. NC State's dedicated page carries an alphabetized Common Name(s) list of three entries -- Common Snowdrop, Snowdrop, Snowdrops -- leading with "Common Snowdrop", and RHS's Plant Profile subtitle, directly beneath the H1 "Galanthus nivalis", gives "common snowdrop" (lowercase). Missouri Botanical Garden's single structured Common Name field, by contrast, reads only "snowdrop"; its longer alternate-names list lives only in an overlib popup and is not quoted here. Two of the three dedicated single-species pages lead with "Common Snowdrop", so that name is used. NC State also carries an "is often confused with" module on this species' page listing, as stacked entries, Galanthus elwesii, Ipheion uniflorum, Leucojum aestivum and Scilla mischtschenkoana. Two of those share the label from the source side: NC State's dedicated Galanthus elwesii page lists "Giant Snowdrop" and "Snowdrop" as that sibling species' names, and its dedicated Leucojum aestivum page lists "Lodden Lily", "Snowflake" and "Summer Snowflake" for Leucojum, a different genus in the same family. Clemson HGIC's dedicated Leucojum page makes the same point from the other side.
records.toxicity_detail: RHS's "Potentially harmful" field for this species names dogs and cats specifically: "Humans/Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". NC State's poison data is human-scoped -- its Problems field lists only "Poisonous to Humans" and the page carries no Problem-for-Cats, Problem-for-Dogs or Problem-for-Horses tag -- and gives Poison Severity Low, Poison Symptoms "Causes low toxicity if eaten in quantity; can result in nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.", Poison Toxic Principle "Phenanthridine alkaloids", and a Poison Part list of Flowers, Leaves and Roots. The same NC State page names a part that list omits: its Edibility field states "Bulbs are toxic if eaten". NC State also carries "Poisonous" as one of the three values of its Plant Type field (Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous) and tags the page "#poisonous". Admissible sources disagree on the contact hazard: NC State answers "Causes Contact Dermatitis: No", while Missouri Botanical Garden's Problems paragraph reads "No serious insect or disease problems. Wear gloves when planting bulbs to avoid possible skin irritation." and RHS instructs gloves in the statement above.
unknowns: No admissible source scopes toxicity to horses; RHS's toxicity statement names only dogs and cats, so toxic_to_pets=true rests on cat/dog evidence alone and no horse-scoped claim is made.
No admissible source names lycorine or galantamine specifically; NC State's Poison Toxic Principle is stated only as the broader category 'Phenanthridine alkaloids.'

No admissible source warns that snowdrop bulbs are mistaken for edible onion bulbs in storage, despite NC State's Description noting the species sits in the Amaryllidaceae (onion) family taxonomically -- that is a family classification, not a storage-confusion warning, so it was not used to support that claim.

chill_damage_f and cool_rest_note left null: NC State's own dedicated species page carries the only on-taxon cold figure, in its Description -- "In order to germinate, snowdrop seeds need to experience a cold spell, below 20 degrees F; therefore, the plant may have a shorter lifespan in warmer climates." That scopes the sub-20F cold spell to SEED GERMINATION, and a germination requirement is neither a blooming requirement nor a damage-onset temperature, so it cannot populate either field. An earlier draft reached for a Penn State Master Gardener page covering G. nivalis and G. elwesii together; that off-taxon multi-species page is dropped.

soil_ph_min/max left null: RHS's pH field lists Acid, Alkaline, and Neutral together (essentially the full range), so no meaningful ceiling or floor could be set from it, and NC State's species page carries no Soil pH field at all.

water_regime left null: no admissible species-specific page gives an explicit watering-cadence statement. MoBot's structured Water field reads 'Medium' (mid-scale) and RHS's Moisture field ('Moist but well-drained or Well-drained') describes soil character, not a watering statement, so neither supports keep_moist.

RHS's structured Position field lists only 'Partial shade' for this species (unlike NC State and MoBot, which both include full sun); outdoor_sun_exposure includes full_sun on the strength of the two agreeing sources, with RHS's narrower field noted here.

No admissible source discusses humidity, day/night temperature ranges, foot-candle light levels, or a fertilizing schedule for this in-ground perennial bulb, so those fields are left null per the instruction to leave day-interval and dry-down fields null for in-ground plants absent explicit framing.
mature_height_in and mature_spread_in taken from NC State Plant Toolbox's structured Dimensions block for this exact species page (galanthus-nivalis), not a genus page or cultivar figure.

is_edible set false because NC State's Edibility field states 'Bulbs are toxic if eaten'; the same page also rates it 'low severity poison characteristics' and lists 'Poisonous to Humans' under Problems -- consistent with a non-edible determination, not a conditional-edibility case.
attracts_pollinators set true from NC State's structured Attracts field, which lists Bees (an unconditional wildlife-attraction field, not seed predation or deer browsing).
Galanthus nivalis is a bulb/herbaceous perennial, not a vine, liana, or other climber, so the climber-exclusion rule for size fields does not apply and all four size fields were populated normally.

The other listed pages (RHS, Missouri Botanical PlantFinder, Clemson HGIC, and the NC State pages for Galanthus elwesii and Leucojum aestivum) were not needed as sources: the anchor NC State Galanthus nivalis page already carried a complete species-level Dimensions block plus Edibility and Attracts fields, so no genus-level or other-species substitute was used for any of the six fields.

Symptoms may include irritation of skin and eyes from cell sap. NC State's anchor page (Agapanthus praecox) states under Poison Symptoms: 'Poisonous through ingestion and dermatitis.  Symptoms may include irritation of skin and eyes from cell sap. Irritation and ulceration of mouth if ingested.' Poison Severity is listed as Low, Poison Part as Leaves, Causes Contact Dermatitis as Yes, and Poison Toxic Principle as Unknown. Literal searches for 'Edible' and 'Pollinator' on the NC State anchor page returned 0 hits; the attracts_pollinators=true and is_edible=false conclusions instead come from the page's Wildlife Value/Attracts fields and Poison Symptoms field respectively, not those literal words.

https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/zantedeschia-aethiopica/ was fetched as instructed but describes an entirely different species (Zantedeschia aethiopica, Calla Lily/Arum Lily), not Agapanthus praecox. It contains no usable data for this record's six fields and was not used for any of them.

Agapanthus praecox is a clump-forming herbaceous perennial, not a vine/climber and not a named cultivar in the sourced text, so the cultivar-exclusion and climber-exclusion rules do not apply and both size dimensions were recorded normally.

NC State also notes a Problems field of 'Poisonous to Humans' and an Attracts field of 'Hummingbirds' (a Design Feature/Attracts sub-block distinct from the Wildlife Value sentence used for the pollinator citation) -- consistent with, and additional support for, the attracts_pollinators=true and is_edible=false calls above.
